submission.natural_language_explanation: This is a word-form detector, not a meaning detector: it fires on a word-initial (sometimes word-internal) piece of a longer multi-token word - 'th' in thousands/fronthaul, ' upl' in uplink, ' append' in appendices, ' embro' in embroidery, ' sym' in symphony, ' hip' in hip-hop, ' upside' in upside-down, 'incre' in incremented, 'appre' in apprendono - and on a specific set of whole content-word tokens: ordinals and comparatives/superlatives (second, third, ... tenth, taller, shortest, deepest, highest), rank/position nouns (top, bottom, upper, middle), and concrete domain nouns (chicken, banana, tomato, sauce, farm, crops, income, savings, trading, music, melody, song, poetry, basket, beacon, mast), regardless of their meaning in context ('wooden top' and 'top of the mountain' both fire). It stays near zero on function words, on common basic-level object/place/person words (table, dog, book, car, door, window, hand, number, teacher, report) and on generic multi-token prefixes (un-, psych-, extra-, mis-).

adversarial_test_results.prompt: On a grey morning in late autumn, the maintenance crew arrived at the reservoir to inspect the intake screens before the winter rains. The supervisor, a patient woman named Alvarez, handed out clipboards and reminded everyone to log the depth readings at each gauge. They walked along the concrete lip of the basin, past valves and pipes, pausing where rust had eaten into a railing. A pump hummed inside the pump house, and the smell of wet cement hung in the air. Alvarez noted that the seals on the east gate needed replacing and that a new gasket had been ordered from a supplier in the valley. Nobody argued; the schedule was tight, and the rains would arrive long before the work was done. Further along the service road, a group of volunteers was clearing brush from a drainage channel that had clogged during the dry season. They piled the cuttings beside the fence and loaded them onto a trailer pulled by a small tractor. One of the volunteers, a retired teacher, joked about the number of spiders living under the stones and shook them from her gloves. The foreman counted the bags, wrote a note in his book, and waved the trailer toward the gate. A dog barked from a yard across the lane, then went quiet. By noon the fog had burned off and the valley looked ordinary again: green slopes, a scatter of roofs, a line of pylons carrying cables toward the coast. The crew ate lunch on the tailgate of a truck, swapping sandwiches and complaints about the forecast. Someone mentioned a leak reported near the old mill, and the supervisor promised to send a team once the reservoir work was finished. The conversation drifted to football, then to a wedding planned for the spring, and then to the price of fuel. In the afternoon they tested the emergency valve. It opened slowly, as it was designed to do, and water spilled into the spillway with a noise like applause. The gauge climbed, hesitated, and settled. Alvarez watched it for a long while, then nodded and wrote the figure in her log. The crew closed the valve, gathered their tools, and drove back along the ridge road with the windows down. Behind them the basin lay quiet under a widening sky, and the pumps went on humming to themselves. At the depot they unloaded the gear into a shed that smelled of oil and rope. A clerk signed for the tools, complaining that the paperwork had changed again and that nobody had told him where the new forms were kept. The foreman promised to look into it and then drove home through the outskirts, past car lots and shuttered shops and a bakery that was still open. He bought bread, milk, and a newspaper, and read the headlines in the car before starting the engine. The news was the usual mixture of weather, sport, and politics, and he put the paper aside after a page or two. That evening the rain finally came, softly at first and then in earnest, drumming on the roof and running down the gutters. He stood by the kitchen window and watched the street turn dark and glossy, and he wondered about the screens at the reservoir and the gasket that had not yet arrived. The forecast promised more of the same for the rest of the week, and he made a mental note to call the supplier in the morning. Then he sat down with his tea, listened to the water in the pipes, and forgot about the meeting entirely.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The town hall filled early on a Tuesday in March, long before the meeting was scheduled to begin. Residents stood along the back wall clutching printed agendas, while the clerk set out water pitchers and adjusted the microphone. Outside, rain drummed on the portico and ran in sheets down the steps. A woman in a yellow coat asked whether the hearing would be recorded and posted online, and the clerk assured her that it would be, as it had been for years. The chair called the session to order, read the minutes of the previous meeting, and asked whether anyone objected. Nobody did, and the minutes were accepted without discussion. The finance director then walked the room through the draft budget line by line. Road repairs would cost more than expected because the winter had been harsh, and the contractor had added a surcharge for emergency work. Library hours would stay the same, but the book fund would shrink, and the parks department would postpone a planned playground. Several residents raised their hands. A retired postal worker asked why the water rates had climbed again. The director explained, patiently, that the old pipes were failing and that borrowing now was cheaper than rebuilding later. Then came the part everyone had been waiting for. The director projected a slide showing the estimated income from the rented stalls in the depot, the savings from sharing equipment with the school kitchen, and the cost of the renovation itself. She put the figures side by side, with the top line showing the total and the bottom line showing the shortfall. A grocer on the corner said she supported the plan. A landlord two doors down said the parking would be a disaster, and the second row of the audience murmured in agreement. The debate went back and forth for nearly an hour, and twice the chair had to ask people to speak one at a time. A student described how her family had used a food bank the previous winter, and the room went quiet. An engineer noted that the building needed a new roof before anything else could be done. The director agreed and said the roof would be handled separately, in the next budget cycle. Near the end, the chair asked for a show of hands on the amended motion. The ayes had it, though not by much, and the clerk recorded the vote in the ledger. On the steps afterward, the grocer caught up with the engineer and asked whether the roof money would come out of the same fund. The engineer shrugged and said nobody knew yet, and the two of them stood under the portico watching the rain while the last of the audience drifted toward their cars. Someone laughed, and someone else promised to bring a cake to the next meeting.

explanation_scores.explanation: This is a word-form detector, not a meaning detector: it fires on a word-initial (sometimes word-internal) piece of a longer multi-token word - 'th' in thousands/fronthaul, ' upl' in uplink, ' append' in appendices, ' embro' in embroidery, ' sym' in symphony, ' hip' in hip-hop, ' upside' in upside-down, 'incre' in incremented, 'appre' in apprendono - and on a specific set of whole content-word tokens: ordinals and comparatives/superlatives (second, third, ... tenth, taller, shortest, deepest, highest), rank/position nouns (top, bottom, upper, middle), and concrete domain nouns (chicken, banana, tomato, sauce, farm, crops, income, savings, trading, music, melody, song, poetry, basket, beacon, mast), regardless of their meaning in context ('wooden top' and 'top of the mountain' both fire). It stays near zero on function words, on common basic-level object/place/person words (table, dog, book, car, door, window, hand, number, teacher, report) and on generic multi-token prefixes (un-, psych-, extra-, mis-).
